questiontext.text: What is the core greedy strategy of Prim's minimum spanning tree algorithm?

answer.text: Grow a single tree from a start vertex, always adding the minimum-weight edge that crosses from the tree to a non-tree vertex

feedback.text: Correct — Prim repeatedly attaches the cheapest crossing edge.

answer.text: Sort all edges globally and add the smallest that avoids a cycle

feedback.text: That is Kruskal's algorithm, not Prim's.

answer.text: Have every component pick its cheapest outgoing edge each round

feedback.text: That is Borůvka's algorithm.

answer.text: Traverse depth-first and keep the first spanning tree encountered

feedback.text: DFS ignores weights, so its spanning tree is not minimum.

generalfeedback.text: Prim keeps one connected tree and, at each step, adds the lightest edge that connects the tree to a vertex not yet in it.

questiontext.text: Which data structure lets Prim efficiently select the next minimum crossing edge?

feedback.text: Correct — the heap returns the cheapest edge/vertex on the frontier.
That is Kruskal's cycle-testing tool, not Prim's selector.
A FIFO queue drives BFS; it does not pick minimum-weight edges.
A stack is for DFS; it has no notion of minimum weight.

generalfeedback.text: A min-heap keyed by the cheapest known connection cost lets Prim extract the next minimum crossing edge in logarithmic time.

questiontext.text: With a binary min-heap, what is the time complexity of Prim's algorithm on a graph with V vertices and E edges?

feedback.text: Correct — each of E edge relaxations costs a log V heap update.

answer.text: O(E log E) dominated by a full edge sort

feedback.text: That is Kruskal; Prim uses a heap, not a global sort.
Prim is greedy and polynomial, not brute force.

answer.text: O(V + E) with no priority structure

feedback.text: The heap adds a log factor; plain O(V + E) is BFS/DFS traversal.

generalfeedback.text: With a binary heap Prim runs in O(E log V); a Fibonacci heap improves this to O(E + V log V).

questiontext.text: Prim's algorithm (especially the array/matrix variant) is often a good fit for which kind of graph?

answer.text: Dense graphs, where E is close to V^2

feedback.text: Correct — Prim's vertex-centric growth suits dense graphs well.
MST requires weighted edges; unweighted MST is trivial.
MSTs are defined on undirected weighted graphs.

answer.text: Only trees, which already have no extra edges

feedback.text: A tree is already its own MST; the algorithm targets general graphs.

generalfeedback.text: Because Prim grows outward from one vertex managing per-vertex keys, it is often preferred on dense graphs, whereas Kruskal shines on sparse ones.

questiontext.text: At every step, the set of edges Prim has chosen so far forms a single connected tree (never a disconnected forest).

feedback.text: Correct — Prim always keeps one connected tree, unlike Kruskal's growing forest.
Prim's defining trait is maintaining a single connected tree throughout.

questiontext.text: Prim's algorithm requires first sorting all edges of the graph by weight before it can begin.

feedback.text: No — that is Kruskal; Prim uses a priority queue and never sorts all edges up front.
Correct — Prim pulls the next minimum edge from a heap, without a global pre-sort.

questiontext.text: Prim's correctness rests on the ______ property: the minimum-weight edge crossing any partition of the vertices is safe to add (single English word for that partition).

feedback.text: Correct — the cut property justifies adding the minimum crossing edge.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about Prim's algorithm are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It grows one connected tree, adding the minimum crossing edge each step

feedback.text: Yes — that is exactly Prim's greedy rule.

answer.text: With a binary heap it runs in O(E log V)

feedback.text: Yes — that is the standard binary-heap bound.

answer.text: It uses union-find to reject edges that create cycles

feedback.text: No — that is Kruskal; Prim's single tree never needs union-find.

answer.text: It halves the number of components each round in parallel

feedback.text: No — that describes Borůvka's algorithm.

generalfeedback.text: Prim is a greedy, single-tree, min-heap algorithm running in O(E log V); union-find belongs to Kruskal and round-based component halving to Borůvka.
